newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Rap label Death Row faces probe.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Rap label Death Row faces probe.

text.p: With its founder in jail, its major star murdered and its bookkeeper in hiding, the record label that helped pioneer Gangsta Rap music finds its tangled past is quickly catching up with it.

Since the murder last year of rap star Tupac Shakur, Death Row records has faced problems ranging from lawsuits to a federal investigation into whether it was started with drug money. There is also a probe to find out why one prosecutor's daughter got a $50,000 recording contract with the label.

Death Row would not comment on the probe or the litigation but legal sources said a grand jury has convened in Los Angeles after a long investigation into the label, which delivered a string of multi-platinum Gangsta hits in its heyday. The grand jury will hear allegations of racketeering, links to street gangs and violent crime, drug trafficking and money laundering against the company, the sources said.

The black-owned label suffered another blow in February when its owner, Marion "Suge" Knight, was sentenced to 9 years in prison for violating his parole on assault charges. Federal officials in Los Angeles have been focusing on the relationship between Knight, his lawyer David Kenner and convicted drug dealer Michael "Harry-O" Harris, sources close to the investigation say.
Harris, Knight and Kenner, who is reportedly recovering from heart surgery, were unavailable for comment.

"Harris has said he was cheated out of money. That is what I and others have heard him saying for years and based on what I know there is no reason to disbelieve him," a Harris associate familiar with the investigation said.
A LOAN FROM JAIL?

Sources said Harris, serving a 28-year sentence, claims he put up $1.5 million to launch Death Row during a visit from Knight and Kenner while he was behind bars in 1991 and that he was cheated out of millions of dollars in profits. Harris has been moved from a state prison to Los Angeles, fanning speculation he will testify before the grand jury.
Questions about its financial dealings have dogged the label since its start and they intensified after Shakur was shot to death in Las Vegas while in a car with Knight.
"The label's future is obviously dubious with Knight out of commission," one executive at a major label said.

Greg Howard, a Death Row spokesman, told Reuters the company was still producing records and is being run by Knight's brother-in-law, Norris Anderson. Interscope Records, a successful label that is half-owned by Seagram Co Ltd, continues to distribute Death Row records but declined to comment on its relationship with the rap label.
Death Row racked up an estimated $300 million in sales but never turned a profit because of large debts and Knight's extravagent spending habits, lawyers and other sources said.

Shakur's mother, Afeni Shakur, a former Black Panther activist, has gone after the label since learning her son died $4.9 million dollars in debt despite having sold more than than $60 million worth of records. She filed a lawsuit against Death Row, Knight and Kenner in April seeking $150 million in damages and says the two sides are currently in negotiations.
"We believe Death Row withheld royalty payments from Tupac and failed to deliver advances promised under his contract," Shakur's lawyer Richard Fischbein told Reuters.
VIOLENCE CONTINUES
The label continues to be dogged by violence. Last month, an employee was shot in a drive-by shooting. And there is the case of the missing accountant.

Coopers & Lybrand, Death Row's former auditors, have turned over all records handled by bookkeeper Steve Cantrock. The firm declined to comment on his whereabouts but sources said he went into hiding after threats on his life.

Other heads have rolled. The state attorney general's office is investigating Los Angeles Deputy District Attorney Lawrence Longo, who oversaw Knight's probation and was discharged on March 31 for conflict of interest. Among the allegations against Longo are that his teenage daughter signed a $50,000 record deal with Death Row and that Longo leased his home to Kenner, Knight's attorney.

"Longo was the prosecutor in Suge Knight's case and the evidence shows that Longo's family trust rented his Malibu home to David Kenner -- the defence attorney for Knight -- and that he knew Marion Knight was going to be the primary occupant of the beach house," Steve Sowders, a spokesman for the Los Angeles District Attorney's office, said.
"Therein lies the conflict. He was prosecuting him while he had him as a tenant for $20,000 a month," Sowders said.
Hearings on Longo's reinstatement have been scheduled in August and September. Among the witnesses being subpoenaed are Knight's attorney, Kenner, a central link to Death Row's saga.
(VO.TO)
